Puzzle 9 · 10 of 23

Two ways to free memory

Your shared Kotlin runs inside an iOS app. Kotlin's objects are freed one way, Swift's another. Here's what happens where they hold on to each other.

  • Puzzle 3: A promise and its keepers

    An expect declaration in common code is a promise; every platform's source set keeps it with an actual declaration. The compiler checks that every target has one. For anything bigger, an interface implemented per platform does the same job and is easier to test.

    Review puzzle 3

  • Puzzle 8: Weak references and closures

    A weak reference points at an object without adding to its count, so it can't keep it alive; it becomes nil when the object is freed. Make one link in a cycle weak and the cycle can be freed. Closures, Swift's lambdas, hold strong references to what they use, including self, so a closure stored by the object it captures is a cycle; [weak self] makes that capture weak. deinit runs when an object is freed.

    Review puzzle 8

The problem

Puzzle 7 showed the two ways to free memory: Kotlin/Native traces from the roots, Swift counts. Now they meet. A Swift view controller holds your Kotlin view model, and the view model keeps a callback, a Swift closure, that points back at the screen. Who frees what, and when?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Kotlin/Native keeps its objects in a shared heap, one pool any thread can use, and frees them with the tracing GC from puzzle 7. Swift objects are freed by reference counting (ARC), also from puzzle 7.

Where the two meet, each side follows its own rules:

  • A Kotlin object that Swift holds stays alive while Swift holds it: to the GC, Swift's hold counts as a root.
  • A Swift object that Kotlin holds isn't freed the moment Kotlin lets go. Releasing the cross-language hold can require a collection and subsequent deinitialization work. Other strong owners can extend the lifetime further. So Swift's deinit can run later than a Swift developer expects.
  • A cycle that runs through both sides, Kotlin to Swift and back, can leak. The GC can't see through Swift's counts, and ARC can't see through Kotlin's references, so neither sees the whole loop, and the cross-language ownership remains live.

The fix is puzzle 8's: make one link weak. Usually the Swift side holds the Kotlin object normally and the callback refers back to the Swift object weakly: in Swift, capture it with [weak self] in the closure you hand to Kotlin.

The analogy

Two cities that clean their streets differently: one sends a sweeper round every few days (the GC), the other picks up each item the moment its owner lets go (ARC). An item two neighbours from different cities each keep "for the other one" is never picked up by either.

Check yourself

Kotlin holds a Swift object, then lets go. When does Swift's deinit run?

Right. Release follows Kotlin's GC, not the moment of letting go.

Not quite. The hold can be released during collection; there is no fixed deinitialization deadline.

Not quite. Kotlin's hold is released by the collector, so the Swift object may outlive the Kotlin reference.

Why can a cycle through both Kotlin and Swift leak?

Right. Two tools, each seeing half the loop.

Not quite. ARC counts fine; the trouble is the loop that runs through both.

Not quite. The GC runs on iOS too; it just can't see past Swift's hold, which counts as a root.

What's the difference between a tracing GC and ARC?

Right. Search in passes vs count as you go.

Not quite. That's the two swapped.

Not quite. Counting is ARC's way; a tracing GC follows references from the roots.

Sources
  • Kotlin docs: Kotlin/Native memory management ("Objects are stored in a shared heap and can be accessed from any thread. Tracing garbage collection is performed periodically to collect objects that are not reachable from the 'roots', like local and global variables.")
  • Kotlin docs: Integration with Swift/Objective-C ARC ("An object is reclaimed only during the garbage collection. This applies to Swift/Objective-C objects that cross interop boundaries into Kotlin/Native"; "To avoid retain cycles, use weak or unowned references")

What you now know

Cross-language ownership can delay deinitialization beyond the point where Kotlin stops using an object. Strong references spanning Kotlin and Swift can form a cycle. Break an ownership link according to the intended lifetime.
